findings.quote: Tolerable risk appetite : Cambridgeshire County Council has defined its maximum risk appetite as not accepting a residual risk score of 16 or more as measured on the corporate Risk Scoring Matrix.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 - Appendix 1 - Annual Risk Management Report 2025-26
findings.headline: SEND statutory delivery and DSG funding risk escalated to corporate register at maximum tolerable risk level.
findings.detail: Risk 15 'Non-delivery of SEND statutory timelines, financial risk of the DfE Safety Valve Agreement for Cambridgeshire and increase in DSG spend' was added to the corporate risk register with a score of 20, matching the council's maximum tolerable risk appetite threshold. The DfE Safety Valve programme ends 31 March 2026, replaced by a 'stability grant' covering 90% of the historic deficit, but continuation depends on submission of a SEND Reform Plan by 19 June 2026. Additional government funding streams remain pending confirmation.
findings.matters: SEND funding volatility, reliance on government programmes, and financial exposure for any amount not covered by the stability grant creates uncertainty about the council's ability to meet its special education commitments.
findings.figures: Risk score 20 at June 2026, stability grant covers up to 90% of historic deficit
findings.quote: The DfE have written to all local authorities within the Safety Valve programme confirming that this will cease on 31st March 2026 and that there will now be arrangements through a 'stability grant' to cover up to 90% of the historic deficit subject to the submission of Cambridgeshire County Council's SEND Reform Plan by 19th June 2026.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: Provider market pressures continue with rising fee rates and National Insurance cost increases
findings.detail: Care provider inflation continues to exceed council budget assumptions. Both existing package uplifts and new placements cost more. Employers National Insurance changes add to pressure. Market for high-need placements is particularly constrained.
findings.matters: These are structural cost pressures beyond the council's control that erode savings plans and create ongoing budget pressure. Unlike demand reduction savings (which can be delivered), provider cost inflation is inevitable.
findings.figures: No specific figures; described as 'continued to be felt'
findings.quote: pressures with the provider market continued to be felt, particularly related to increasing fee rates, and changes in employers National Insurance commitments. The impacts of inflationary pressures are seen both in the uplifts required for existing care packages, and the price at which new packages are sourced; and the position of the care market, particularly around specific types of provision and location, continues to make some placements more difficult to source, particularly for those people with higher needs.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: Systematic failure of savings delivery, with £3.9m variance on £28.3m planned (14% shortfall)
findings.detail: Multiple multi-year savings initiatives failed or under-delivered: Digital Innovation (£300k black), Learning Disability schemes (£391k+£187k black status), review of discharge pathways (£598k red), in-house provision review (£1m black). Many savings carried forward from prior years are still not delivering, indicating structural delivery problems.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if savings plans can be executed. Systematic failure across multiple initiatives and multiple years shows the council has difficulty delivering efficiency targets.
findings.figures: £3,966k variance on £28,312k planned savings (14% shortfall)
findings.quote: In addition to the pressures on services for people with Learning Disabilities, there remain a number of challenging savings targets from 2024-25 and 2025-26 which have not delivered in full in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: ICB withdrew funding for statutory Section 12 Mental Health Assessments mid-year, creating unfunded obligation
findings.detail: In May 2025, the ICB stopped funding Section 12 assessments that are statutorily required for Deprivation of Liberty safeguards. The council became solely responsible. This created a £103k pressure in Safeguarding, and the council has had to build funding into the 2026-27 business plan.
findings.matters: A statutory obligation with no funding source represents a cost the council cannot avoid. This mid-year funding withdrawal by a partner shows partnership funding is unreliable.
findings.figures: £103k in-year overspend from May onwards
findings.quote: The 2025-26 overspend of £103k is due to the in-year impact of the ICB withdrawing funding for Section 12 Mental Health Assessments (S12) in May 2025. The Council is now solely responsible for funding these assessments, which are a statutory requirement for issuing lawful Deprivation of Liberty safeguards (DoLS) authorisations.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: Independent Living Service capital scheme closed after failed NHS negotiations, writing off £459k in costs
findings.detail: A planned capital scheme was closed after 12 months of negotiation with the NHS failed to reach agreement on funding terms. No alternative option was identified. The £459k in abortive costs was written back to revenue, damaging 2025-26 outturn and reducing capital programme efficiency.
findings.matters: A lender funds capital programmes; schemes that fail after costs are incurred show poor project management and indicate other capital schemes may also be at risk.
findings.figures: £459k abortive costs written to revenue
findings.quote: Abortive costs of £459k from the Independent Living Service: East Cambridgeshire have been written back to revenue following closure of the scheme.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: Adult social care debt has grown to £24.8m with £12.6m overdue over one year, up 35% from prior year
findings.detail: Overdue debt grew from £24.4m in February to £24.8m in March. Debt over one year old stands at £12.6m compared to £9.3m at end of March 2024. This creates collection risk and required a £1.7m provision in accounts (£1m borne by this directorate), indicating the council doubts it will recover significant sums.
findings.matters: Growing uncollectable debt signals either deteriorating ability of service users to pay or declining collection effort. Either way, a lender would see rising credit risk and structural pressure on council finances.
findings.figures: £24.8m total overdue (up from £24.4m); £12.6m over one year old (£9.3m in prior year)
findings.quote: Adults, Health and Commissioning overdue debt (excluding debt with Health partners) stood at £24.8m at the end of March, up from £24.4m at the end of February... This compares to a balance of £9.3m at the end of March 2024. As such, the position on adult social care debt remains challenging and this presents risks both in terms of potential non-payment and the requirement to make a risk-assessed provision within the accounts.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Appendix 1 - Adults Health and Commissioning Finance Monitoring Report - Outturn 2025-26 2026
findings.headline: Learning Disability pooled budget ending failed to deliver £2.1m of expected savings
findings.detail: The council planned for £2.4m savings when the ICB pooled budget ended in March 2025, but achieved only £320k. The original budget was overestimated on health needs, and joint funded packages are now at lower levels than expected. Corporate funding of £2.9m was allocated to mitigate the shortfall, but savings shortfalls are now built into 2026-27 planning.
findings.matters: A massive undelivered saving (87% shortfall on a material amount) indicates serious budget planning failures and ongoing structural pressure in the council's largest service area.
findings.figures: Planned saving £2,387k, achieved £320k, variance £2,067k (87%)
findings.quote: The ending of the pooled budget arrangements was expected to reduce costs for the Council and savings were built into previous Business Plans to reflect this; but the actual impact is not achieving those savings in full.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Finance Monitoring Report (Outturn 2025-26)
findings.headline: Babraham Park and Ride solar site experienced five-month outage due to cable fault, and St Ives EV charger uptake slower than expected despite fix.
findings.detail: Babraham Park and Ride solar connection was delayed five months following a cable fault, resulting in zero income during that period (£397k impact). The cable was fixed and the site energised in October 2025. St Ives Park and Ride EV chargers also experienced delays; uptake has been slower than expected and additional communications are planned. These are operational/delivery failures on council-owned infrastructure that are consuming management time to remediate.
findings.matters: Park and Ride sites are public-facing infrastructure with income generation expectations. Five-month outages and lower-than-expected EV uptake suggest either poor project execution, poor demand forecasting, or both; this pattern echoes across the energy portfolio.
findings.figures: £397k income loss from five-month Babraham outage; EV charger delay at St Ives; uptake described as slower than anticipated
findings.quote: The delayed connection date for the Babraham Park and Ride site following a cable fault, resulted in five months with no income from solar generation at this site. However, the cable is now fixed, and the site was energised in October 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Finance Monitoring Report (Outturn 2025-26)
findings.headline: £2,530k of earmarked reserves drawn down to balance the outturn position, representing material reliance on one-off funding rather than structural balance.
findings.detail: To achieve a balanced outturn, the council released £2,530k from earmarked reserves. This includes £624k from parking reserves, £250k from a one-off National Highways A14 adoption payment, £570k from Infrastructure & Project Delivery for completed projects, £500k to replace base budget in Communities, £585k Just Transition Funding returned but reallocated, and £150k planned draw not needed. While described as planned, the breadth and materiality of these drawdowns indicates structural reliance on reserves rather than operating within baseline revenue.
findings.matters: A borrowing council in structural deficit relative to base budgets signals weakening financial sustainability. Reserves provide a buffer but deplete over time; if baseline revenue cannot cover operating costs, the council will face increasing pressure.
findings.figures: £2,530k total earmarked reserve drawdown in 2025-26; composed of multiple £250k-£624k tranches across different services
findings.quote: As reported through the year, planned drawdowns from reserves were actioned as mitigations to the Place & Sustainability and overall council financial position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Finance Monitoring Report (Outturn 2025-26)
findings.headline: On-street parking income fell £1,077k short of budget; reserve drawdown used to partly mitigate with no full offset planned for 2026-27.
findings.detail: On-street pay and display income was substantially lower than budgeted in 2025-26. The council drew down £624k from the on-street parking reserve to partially fund this pressure, but explicitly chose not to fully offset the overspend in order to preserve the reserve balance for managing the 2026-27 position. This signals the council expects continued income pressure on parking in the next financial year.
findings.matters: A £1m shortfall on a recurring income stream, combined with an explicit decision to preserve contingency rather than offset it, suggests the council expects structural income pressure and is managing down expectations rather than addressing root causes.
findings.figures: £1,077k underachievement; £624k reserve drawdown; decision made not to fully offset to manage 2026-27 reserve balance
findings.quote: Parking Enforcement: a £1,077k underachievement of income is reported for 25-26 due to on-street pay and display income being substantially lower than budgeted. Please note that this position is partly mitigated in 2025-26 through the use of the parking reserve.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Finance Monitoring Report (Outturn 2025-26)
findings.headline: Energy income savings collapsed across all three projects: combined £3,565k planned savings achieved only £1,959k (45% delivery).
findings.detail: The 2025-30 Business Plan included three energy schemes as savings. North Angle (£3,565k planned, £1,959k delivered, RED rating), St Ives Smart Energy Grid (£73k planned, £0 delivered, BLACK rating), and Babraham Smart Energy Grid (£462k planned, £68k delivered plus £85k planned, £0 delivered; both Amber/BLACK). The savings were income-dependent and relied on availability and uptake of EV chargers and grid connections, all of which experienced delays and lower-than-expected performance.
findings.matters: A lender approves borrowing partly on planned savings delivery; a 45% achievement on a £3.5m savings target indicates either poor forecasting or systemic market issues (EV uptake, network constraints) that may affect the council's ability to deliver future infrastructure income targets.
findings.figures: North Angle: £3,565k planned / £1,959k delivered (45%); St Ives: £73k planned / £0 delivered; Babraham: combined planned £547k / delivered £68k (12%)
findings.quote: Lower than forecast income due to curtailment of generation by the DNO

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Finance Monitoring Report (Outturn 2025-26)
findings.headline: North Angle solar farm curtailment is costing material income: £1,356k loss in 2025-26 due to electricity network capacity constraint.
findings.detail: The North Angle solar farm has experienced more significant curtailment of exports by the electricity network operator than anticipated. The network does not have the capacity to absorb all generation during peak hours, and officers are reviewing commercial and engineering measures. This represents a structural problem with the site's income generation, not a one-off issue, as the network capacity constraint is the root cause.
findings.matters: A lender funding capital infrastructure expects revenue generation to meet debt repayment; an income loss of this scale on a strategic asset signals either overly optimistic underwriting or a systemic constraint on the site's performance.
findings.figures: £1,356k income loss on North Angle in 2025-26; total energy projects overspend £1,774k (366% variance on £484k net budget)
findings.quote: North Angle solar farm has experienced much more significant curtailment of exports by the electricity operator than anticipated, as the network doesn't have the capacity to absorb all the generation during peak hours.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Maintained schools show increasing deficit trend: 38 schools in deficit at March 2026, cumulative deficit of £6.76m, up from 37 schools and £3.93m prior year
findings.detail: The number of maintained schools reporting deficit budgets increased from 37 to 38, with cumulative deficit value nearly doubling from £3.93m to £6.76m. While the council still holds a cumulative net balance of £13.09m across all schools, the trend is deteriorating. The report notes schools are completing their 2026-27 budget setting and further details on deficit schools will be shared in due course.
findings.matters: An increasing number of schools in deficit, with deficit values rising sharply year-on-year, signals that schools are under financial stress and may require council intervention or bailout; this is a contingent liability.
findings.figures: Schools in deficit March 2026: 38 (March 2025: 37), cumulative deficit £6.76m (March 2025: £3.93m), cumulative net balance across all schools £13.09m
findings.quote: Appendix 6 shows a summary of the revenue balance position as at 31st March for maintained schools. Schools are currently completing their budget setting for 2026-27 and as such further details on the numbers of schools setting deficit budgets will be shared in due course.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Children's Disability Service overspent by £974k due to demand and complexity in Community Support Service, with increasing Direct Payments for high-cost support packages
findings.detail: The 0-25 Disability Service overspent by £974k, with ongoing pressures from demand and complexity in the Community Support Service and community clubs. The change in position from previous reporting is due to increased spend on Direct Payments for a new high-cost support package. Work is ongoing to manage delivery of community support but is being offset by increased spend supporting complex children and young people.
findings.matters: A £974k overspend on Disability Services driven by individual high-cost packages signals an inability to manage demand or gate-keep expensive interventions; this is a growing area of risk.
findings.figures: Children's Disability Service overspend £974k (11% of budget of £9.245m)
findings.quote: The 0-25 Disability Service's final position saw overspend increase to £974k. Ongoing pressures are due to demand and complexity in the Community Support Service and Camplay holiday, Saturday and community clubs. Work continues to take place around the delivery of community support, with some changes being made to try and minimise the risk of overspend into the new financial year.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Core non-DSG services overspent by £11.32m (7.3% of budget), with major pressures in Education (£3.935m), Commissioning/Placements (£8.445m), and Disability Services (£974k)
findings.detail: The overall non-DSG overspend of £11.32m on a net budget of £154.121m was driven by Children in Care Placements (£8.462m), Education services (£3.935m including Home to School Transport of £2.943m), and Children's Disability Service (£974k). These represent demand-led pressures rather than controllable cost variances.
findings.matters: A 7.3% overspend on non-DSG budgets across multiple demand-led services indicates the council is not managing demand pressures effectively and may face recurring deficits in these areas.
findings.figures: Total non-DSG overspend £11.323m on budget of £154.121m (7.3%), Children in Care £8.462m, Education £3.935m, Disability £974k
findings.quote: At the end of 2025-26, Children, Education and Families (CEF) overspent by £11.32m on core funded activities and £33.74m overspent on Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) activities.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Savings delivery fell short by £1.652m (10% variance), with several planned savings rated 'Black' (not delivered) including £1.231m Residential Strategy saving
findings.detail: Out of £16.47m planned savings for 2025-26, only £14.818m were delivered. Savings rated 'Black' (not delivered) include Social Care and Education Transport (£89k), Home to School Transport (£63k), and Residential Strategy (£1.231m), the latter due to implementation delays. The Residential Strategy saving failure is partly mitigated by £650k associated investment not being required. Several savings rated 'Red' or 'Amber' show partial delivery only.
findings.matters: A 10% shortfall in planned savings, with material items rated 'Black' (not achieved), suggests the council's savings delivery capability is weak and planned actions may not land; this is material given the structural budget deficits.
findings.figures: Total savings planned £16.47m, achieved £14.818m, variance £1.652m (10%), Residential Strategy saving not delivered £1.231m
findings.quote: Due to implementation delays it was not possible to deliver this saving in 2025/26. In-year mitigation due to £650k of associated investment not being required due to the implementation delays, resulting in a net budget impact of -£581k.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: High Needs Block overspent by £39.169m due to increasing numbers of EHCPs and complexity of need resulting in higher-cost independent placements
findings.detail: The High Needs Block ended the year with an overspend of £39.169m within the DSG, reflecting the continuing increase in numbers of Education Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and complexity of need. This has resulted in higher cost placements in independent settings and pupils on tuition packages. The report notes this is offset in part by one-off underspends on Schools and Early Years Blocks.
findings.matters: A £39m overspend on High Needs is a structural problem driven by external policy (increasing EHCP identification) that the council cannot control; it is a key driver of the £96m DSG deficit.
findings.figures: High Needs Block overspend £39.169m, out-of-school tuition overspend (DSG) £3.533m, SEN Placements overspend (DSG) £5.250m
findings.quote: The High Needs Block (HNB) ended the year with an overspend of £39.169m, which reflects the continuing increase in numbers of Educations Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) and complexity of need resulting in higher cost placements in independent settings and pupils on tuition packages.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspent by £2.943m, with High Needs transport overspending by £1.673m and Mainstream by £1.137m
findings.detail: Overspend driven by sustained growth in numbers eligible for transport linked to increases in EHCPs, rising cost of securing transport provision due to inflation and contract prices, and shortage of local special school places forcing longer journeys at higher cost. The report identifies this as 'a key area of financial risk requiring continued focus' and notes that whilst earlier forecast overspends have been reduced through mitigation activity, 'the outturn reflects ongoing demand-led and market-driven pressures'.
findings.matters: A £2.943m overspend on demand-led transport, with the council explicitly labelling it a key financial risk requiring continued focus, indicates an uncontrolled cost pressure that is likely to recur and grow alongside EHCP numbers.
findings.figures: Total Home to School Transport overspend £2.943m (Special £1.673m + Mainstream £1.137m + Children in Care £133k)
findings.quote: While the final position shows a marginal improvement compared with earlier forecasts, the outturn reflects ongoing demand-led and market-driven pressures, and Home to School Transport remains a key area of financial risk requiring continued focus.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Children in care placements overspent by £8.462m due to 18 more children than budgeted requiring expensive residential care
findings.detail: Budget assumed 310 placements but 328 children needed care at year-end. The overspend was driven by an increase in demand for residential care, which is typically more expensive than other provisions. The report states that whilst unit costs have been controlled through contract management, demand remains the key pressure. The outturn reduced slightly from previously reported position due to additional health contributions toward care packages.
findings.matters: Demand-driven overspends in children's placements signal a council unable to control one of its largest cost pressures; the 18-placement increase suggests the problem is structural, not cyclical, and may recur if demand continues.
findings.figures: Overspend £8.462m, 328 placements actual vs 310 budgeted (18 more), unregulated placements £5.679k higher than budget
findings.quote: The year end position for children's external placements is an overspend of £8.462m. This budget has been under significant pressure primarily driven by an increase by the demand for residential care which is typically more expensive than most other provisions. As of 31st March 2026, 328 children needed to be cared for in (registered and unregistered) residential care. This is a difference of 18 more children than budgeted for.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 Appendix A - Children Education & Families FMR - Outturn March 2026
findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £96.257m carried forward into 2026-27
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £39.169m in-year, reflecting continuing increases in numbers of Education Health and Care Plans and complexity of need. A revised cumulative DSG deficit of £62.851m was brought forward from prior years, and the final net in-year position adds £33.739m, totalling £96.257m to be carried forward. The report notes this is offset partially by one-off underspends on Schools and Early Years Blocks.
findings.matters: A £96m structural DSG deficit is a material threat to the council's financial sustainability and limits flexibility for other services; it represents a growing liability that must be addressed through savings or government intervention.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit brought forward £62.851m, in-year overspend £33.739m, cumulative total £96.257m
findings.quote: A revised cumulative DSG deficit of £62.851m was brought forward into 2025-26 and the final net in-year DSG position is a £33.739m overspend. Allowing for prior-year adjustments in relation to Early Years the revised cumulative DSG deficit to be carried forward into 2026/27 totals £96.257m.

news_drafts.headline: Traffic signal infrastructure now at or beyond design life with rising obsolescence costs and global supply chain pressures
news_drafts.lead: Assets now at or past design life with mounting obsolescence create uncontrolled replacement demand. Artificial life extension increases failure risk. This asset category will require significant capital spending as forced replacement occurs.

news_drafts.headline: Structures assets held in 'Fair' condition accepting moderate risk to public safety as a financial constraint
news_drafts.lead: Accepting moderate public safety risk due to funding constraints creates liability exposure and reputational risk. This represents a deliberate trade-off of safety for affordability.

news_drafts.headline: Multiple significant asset inventory gaps prevent accurate financial planning and mask the true cost of asset management
news_drafts.lead: Incomplete asset data prevents accurate financial forecasting and creates risk that the £57.967m annual requirement is understated. The council cannot confidently manage assets it has not inventoried, and future costs could be materially higher.
